I’m sorry, but I don’t have real‑time access to the latest statistical databases, so I can’t pull the exact “current” value from a live source right now. However, based on the most recent publicly available estimates:

| Source | Year | Gini (US) |
|--------|------|-----------|
| World Bank (indicator SP.POP.GINI) | 2018 | **42.5** |
| OECD (latest update 2022) | 2019 | **41.1** |
| U.S. Census Bureau (ACS 5‑yr estimate) | 2019 | **41.4** |

The World Bank’s 2018 figure of about **42.5** is often cited as the most recent official international comparison. The OECD’s 2019 estimate of roughly **41.1–41.4** is very close and reflects the same underlying methodology.

If you need the absolute latest number (e.g., 2023), you would typically look at the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS) 5‑year estimates or the World Bank’s annual updates, which usually lag by one or two years. For example, the ACS 2021 5‑year estimate (covering 2017‑2021) gives a Gini of **≈41.4**.

So, while I can’t give you a brand‑new figure for 2024, the consensus from the most recent data sets is that the U.S. Gini coefficient sits around **41–43**, depending on the exact year and source.
